analysis.investment_thesis: Aequs operates in the right sectors (aerospace, defense) with India's manufacturing tailwind, but three consecutive years of net losses, declining 2025 revenue (-4% YoY), and a preposterous 1,140x forward P/E make this uninvestable at current prices. A growth investor demands earnings growth, not loss deepening.
key_strengths: Aerospace & defense contract manufacturing exposure — a sector with durable long-term demand and high barriers to supplier qualification
High gross margins (56.24%) imply value-added manufacturing rather than commodity processing
Large CWIP build (₹395 Cr in FY25, up from zero in FY23) signals capacity investment that could unlock future scale
key_risks: Revenue actually shrank in FY25 (₹965 Cr → ₹925 Cr) while net loss widened to ₹102 Cr — the opposite of the compounding growth Fisher demands
Free cash flow deeply negative and worsening (-₹76 Cr → -₹175 Cr → -₹239 Cr) with capex surging to ₹265 Cr; the company is burning cash at an accelerating rate
D/E of 1.08 and finance costs of ₹64–69 Cr annually create a structural earnings headwind — Fisher's threshold is <0.5
red_flags: Forward P/E of 1,140x on a loss-making company implies the market has priced in perfection that does not yet exist in financials
Business sprawl across unrelated verticals (aerospace + toys + cookware + real estate clusters) violates Fisher's focus principle — great companies do one thing superbly
EBITDA swung from ₹163 Cr (FY24) to ₹57 Cr (FY25) — a 65% collapse — driven partly by ₹44 Cr 'other income' in FY24 reversing to -₹6 Cr in FY25, suggesting low earnings quality
analysis.detailed_analysis:
From my Scuttlebutt perspective, Aequs has built something structurally interesting — vertically integrated manufacturing clusters in Belgaum serving aerospace OEMs. The aerospace and defense contract manufacturing story in India is real: domestic procurement mandates and offset requirements from global primes create genuine long-term demand. The 56% gross margin tells me customers pay for precision engineering, not just labor arbitrage. And CWIP jumping to ₹395 Cr tells me management is betting heavily on future capacity — the kind of bold capital commitment I admire in visionary founders. Promoter holding at 59% provides alignment.

But my checklist demands earnings growth, and this company cannot even deliver stable revenues. Revenue fell 4% in FY25; net losses widened to ₹102 Cr after a brief respite at -₹14 Cr in FY24. Operating margins are negative (-1.84%). Finance costs consume ₹64 Cr annually against an EBITDA of just ₹57 Cr — meaning the company earns nothing after interest. The valuation of 1,140x forward P/E and 288x EV/EBITDA is pure speculation, not growth investing. I can wait for a company to become profitable, but I cannot justify paying today as if it already is. When the facts improve — sustained revenue growth above 20%, positive free cash flow, debt halved — this story deserves another look. Not now.
